The index captures the spatially observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies alongside the intensity with which economic space is used. It is designed for hyper-local sub-national monitoring: it tracks local economic activity and growth, and reveals spatial disparities and regional dynamics that national and state accounts often mask. keenable.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
keenable.snippet: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($\rho$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $\beta$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years.

keenable.title: Nighttime light and India’s urban-economic growth, reference to the global human settlement layer and world settlement footprint in Google Earth Engine
keenable.snippet: socioeconomic statistics and single-indicator remote sensing approaches have limited capacity to resolve the coupled physical, functional, demographic, and economic dimensions of urban growth, particularly at the national scale. This study addresses this gap by integrating nighttime light (NTL), Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), World Settlement Footprint (WSF), and socioeconomic and electricity datasets within Google Earth Engine (GEE) to characterize India’s urban-economic transformation and its major metropolitan growth poles. Multi-temporal DMSP-OLS and VIIRS-DNB (1994–2025) artificial light at night were independently noise-screened, temporally normalized, and spatially harmonized with GHSL built-up surface, building volume, population, degree of urbanization, settlement characteristics, building height, and WSF settlement footprints. Temporal-change analysis, indicator derivation, Pearson correlation, ordinary least-squares regression, and cross-dataset validation were employed on six selected major metropolitan agglomerations, Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad across India. Mean NTL radiance increased from 10.84 to 37.19, representing 243.1% growth, while mean built-up surface increased from 10.27 to 41.45 m2 pixel−1 and built-up volume from 91.68 to 266.52 m3 pixel−1. NTL exhibited strong associations with built-up surface (R2 = 0.9463), GDP (R2 = 0.8353), population (R2 = 0.8045), and building volume (R2 = 0.7644). Long-term increases in energy and electricity consumption provided complementary evidence of growing urban economic activity. Cross-dataset consistency was also substantial between NTL and GHSL (*r* = 0.884). The integrated framework demonstrates that combining functional illumination with physical, demographic, and economic indicators can provide a scalable basis for evidence-based urban monitoring, infrastructure prioritization, and sustainable spatiotemporal planning in rapidly transforming urban systems.

keenable.title: Tracking Socio-Economic Development in Rural India over Two Decades Using Satellite Imagery
keenable.snippet: Indicators of socio-economic development based on satellite data have emerged as a proxy to track development at fine spatial and temporal scales. We build a model using daytime and nightlights satellite data to estimate an index of socio-economic development at the village level in India. We evaluate our model for temporal robustness and use it to produce estimates at three time points over a two-decade period. We then use these estimates to understand the effect on village-level development of factors such as the geographic distance of a village to hubs of economic activity and the inequality of development in the district. Our findings provide evidence of the possible impact that policy changes during this period have had on village development.

keenable.title: Regional growth, convergence, and spatial spillovers in India: A reproducible view from outer space
keenable.snippet: Using satellite nighttime light data as a proxy for economic activity, Chanda and Kabiraj (2020, World Development) studied regional growth and convergence across 520 districts in India. Adopting a reproducible open-science approach, this article builds on their work by extending their main findings on three empirical fronts. First, we illustrate regional convergence patterns using an interactive tool for satellite imagery visualization. Second, we assess the degree of spatial dependence in their main econometric specification. Third, we employ a spatial Durbin model to measure the role of spatial spillovers in the convergence process. Our results indicate that spatial spillovers increase the estimated speed of regional convergence. In our fully specified model, spillovers raise the convergence speed from about 3.0% to about 5.2% per year, which shortens the half-life of regional disparities from roughly 23 to 13 years.

keenable-realtime.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
keenable-realtime.snippet: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($\rho$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $\beta$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years.

keenable-realtime.snippet: socioeconomic statistics and single-indicator remote sensing approaches have limited capacity to resolve the coupled physical, functional, demographic, and economic dimensions of urban growth, particularly at the national scale. This study addresses this gap by integrating nighttime light (NTL), Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), World Settlement Footprint (WSF), and socioeconomic and electricity datasets within Google Earth Engine (GEE) to characterize India’s urban-economic transformation and its major metropolitan growth poles. Multi-temporal DMSP-OLS and VIIRS-DNB (1994–2025) artificial light at night were independently noise-screened, temporally normalized, and spatially harmonized with GHSL built-up surface, building volume, population, degree of urbanization, settlement characteristics, building height, and WSF settlement footprints. Temporal-change analysis, indicator derivation, Pearson correlation, ordinary least-squares regression, and cross-dataset validation were employed on six selected major metropolitan agglomerations, Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad across India. Mean NTL radiance increased from 10.84 to 37.19, representing 243.1% growth, while mean built-up surface increased from 10.27 to 41.45 m2 pixel−1 and built-up volume from 91.68 to 266.52 m3 pixel−1. NTL exhibited strong associations with built-up surface (R2 = 0.9463), GDP (R2 = 0.8353), population (R2 = 0.8045), and building volume (R2 = 0.7644). Long-term increases in energy and electricity consumption provided complementary evidence of growing urban economic activity. Cross-dataset consistency was also substantial between NTL and GHSL (*r* = 0.884). The integrated framework demonstrates that combining functional illumination with physical, demographic, and economic indicators can provide a scalable basis for evidence-based urban monitoring, infrastructure prioritization, and sustainable spatiotemporal planning in rapidly transforming urban systems.

keenable-realtime.snippet: Indicators of socio-economic development based on satellite data have emerged as a proxy to track development at fine spatial and temporal scales. We build a model using daytime and nightlights satellite data to estimate an index of socio-economic development at the village level in India. We evaluate our model for temporal robustness and use it to produce estimates at three time points over a two-decade period. We then use these estimates to understand the effect on village-level development of factors such as the geographic distance of a village to hubs of economic activity and the inequality of development in the district. Our findings provide evidence of the possible impact that policy changes during this period have had on village development.

keenable-realtime.title: Regional growth, convergence, and spatial spillovers in India: A reproducible view from outer space
keenable-realtime.snippet: Using satellite nighttime light data as a proxy for economic activity, Chanda and Kabiraj (2020, World Development) studied regional growth and convergence across 520 districts in India. Adopting a reproducible open-science approach, this article builds on their work by extending their main findings on three empirical fronts. First, we illustrate regional convergence patterns using an interactive tool for satellite imagery visualization. Second, we assess the degree of spatial dependence in their main econometric specification. Third, we employ a spatial Durbin model to measure the role of spatial spillovers in the convergence process. Our results indicate that spatial spillovers increase the estimated speed of regional convergence. In our fully specified model, spillovers raise the convergence speed from about 3.0% to about 5.2% per year, which shortens the half-life of regional disparities from roughly 23 to 13 years.

A study of the growth rates at local levels using high-resolution daytime satellite imagery data on built-up surfaces, shows significantly higher growth of built-up surface under the Modi years of 2015-2020 than the UPA years of 2010-15. parallel.snippet:
One of the appealing features of night time lights is its availability at the most disaggregated geographical levels. The data is captured through night-time imagery satellite and focuses on establishing a relationship between the inequality indices calculated by income estimates and night time lights. It is measured on a 30 arc sec level, corresponding to roughly 1 square kilometre at the equator. This means that the NTL data could be used to measure economic activities at sub-national-levels which are not usually captured in national accounts such as provinces, districts, towns/cities and villages. The underlying hypothesis being that the light is as good a proxy for calculating regional inequality as it is for income. Thus using the NTL, a new inequality index could be created at granular administrative levels that could be used for designing and implementing policies.
The Gini coefficient is the most commonly used standard measure of economic inequality.

# Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
## Abstract
This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting.
The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used.
Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted.
The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2).

India needs to measure growth where policy meets the ground to help it solve problems such as economic exclusion where they are most keenly felt.

Decisions that matter for growth and welfare are taken at the level of districts, blocks, peri-urban corridors and villages. Yet India’s measurement systems still speak largely in the language of states and national averages. That mismatch creates uncertainty for both governments and firms. Public programmes are designed with imperfect information and private investors make location choices with partial visibility.

India’s official statistics have improved meaningfully. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI) and the National Statistical Office (NSO) have modernised operations, increased transparency and expanded the availability of high-frequency indicators – data that is updated more often. For instance, the redesigned Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) now produces monthly urban labour market indicators and quarterly estimates, giving policy makers a much more up-to-date picture of jobs and employment. This is a major step for economic debates based on current data rather than assumptions.

The remaining gaps concern granularity and local frequency, i.e., how detailed the data is and how often it is updated locally. Most official data observe the economy at the level of states or districts, while implementation happens far below that scale. Investments in physical infrastructure, welfare programmes and logistics networks depend on information that is sharper than a district average and more frequent than a major survey round.

ultimate.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
ultimate.snippet: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($\rho$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $\beta$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years.

ultimate.title: Nighttime light and India’s urban-economic growth, reference to the global human settlement layer and world settlement footprint in Google Earth Engine
ultimate.snippet: socioeconomic statistics and single-indicator remote sensing approaches have limited capacity to resolve the coupled physical, functional, demographic, and economic dimensions of urban growth, particularly at the national scale. This study addresses this gap by integrating nighttime light (NTL), Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), World Settlement Footprint (WSF), and socioeconomic and electricity datasets within Google Earth Engine (GEE) to characterize India’s urban-economic transformation and its major metropolitan growth poles. Multi-temporal DMSP-OLS and VIIRS-DNB (1994–2025) artificial light at night were independently noise-screened, temporally normalized, and spatially harmonized with GHSL built-up surface, building volume, population, degree of urbanization, settlement characteristics, building height, and WSF settlement footprints. Temporal-change analysis, indicator derivation, Pearson correlation, ordinary least-squares regression, and cross-dataset validation were employed on six selected major metropolitan agglomerations, Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad across India. Mean NTL radiance increased from 10.84 to 37.19, representing 243.1% growth, while mean built-up surface increased from 10.27 to 41.45 m2 pixel−1 and built-up volume from 91.68 to 266.52 m3 pixel−1. NTL exhibited strong associations with built-up surface (R2 = 0.9463), GDP (R2 = 0.8353), population (R2 = 0.8045), and building volume (R2 = 0.7644). Long-term increases in energy and electricity consumption provided complementary evidence of growing urban economic activity. Cross-dataset consistency was also substantial between NTL and GHSL (*r* = 0.884). The integrated framework demonstrates that combining functional illumination with physical, demographic, and economic indicators can provide a scalable basis for evidence-based urban monitoring, infrastructure prioritization, and sustainable spatiotemporal planning in rapidly transforming urban systems.

ultimate.title: Tracking Socio-Economic Development in Rural India over Two Decades Using Satellite Imagery
ultimate.snippet: Indicators of socio-economic development based on satellite data have emerged as a proxy to track development at fine spatial and temporal scales. We build a model using daytime and nightlights satellite data to estimate an index of socio-economic development at the village level in India. We evaluate our model for temporal robustness and use it to produce estimates at three time points over a two-decade period. We then use these estimates to understand the effect on village-level development of factors such as the geographic distance of a village to hubs of economic activity and the inequality of development in the district. Our findings provide evidence of the possible impact that policy changes during this period have had on village development.

ultimate.title: Regional growth, convergence, and spatial spillovers in India: A reproducible view from outer space
ultimate.snippet: Using satellite nighttime light data as a proxy for economic activity, Chanda and Kabiraj (2020, World Development) studied regional growth and convergence across 520 districts in India. Adopting a reproducible open-science approach, this article builds on their work by extending their main findings on three empirical fronts. First, we illustrate regional convergence patterns using an interactive tool for satellite imagery visualization. Second, we assess the degree of spatial dependence in their main econometric specification. Third, we employ a spatial Durbin model to measure the role of spatial spillovers in the convergence process. Our results indicate that spatial spillovers increase the estimated speed of regional convergence. In our fully specified model, spillovers raise the convergence speed from about 3.0% to about 5.2% per year, which shortens the half-life of regional disparities from roughly 23 to 13 years.

A long-term satellite monitoring study integrating multi-sensor remote sensing data has quantified the scale and spatial characteristics of urban and economic expansion across India’s primary metropolitan growth poles over a three-decade observation period. Nighttime light radiance demonstrated its strongest linear association with physical built-up surface area, registering an R-squared value of 0.9463.
